variants.title: Learn one merge
variants.context: BPE learns one merge at a time: initialize symbols from characters or bytes with a word-ending marker, count adjacent pairs weighted by word frequency, merge the highest-frequency pair and add it to the vocabulary, then recount and repeat until the budget or minimum-frequency rule stops training.
variants.prompt: A BPE trainer runs. Put one iteration in order.

items.text: Merge the highest-frequency eligible pair everywhere it occurs without overlap and append it to the vocabulary.
Recount from the new segmentation and repeat until the vocabulary budget or minimum frequency stops training.
Initialize symbols: normalize, pre-tokenize, split words into characters or bytes with an end-of-word marker.
Count adjacent pairs inside every sequence, weighted by corpus frequency.

variants.hint: Recount after every merge; bulk-applying top pairs is a different algorithm.
variants.explanation: A merge changes the neighbors visible to the next step.

variants.prompt: Why recount after each merge? Put the iteration in order.

items.text: Count pairs; the previous merge created new adjacent pairs.
Recount again before choosing the next.

variants.explanation: Selecting the top pairs once and applying them in bulk is a different algorithm.

variants.prompt: Training stops. Put the final iteration in order, ending with the stop rule.

items.text: Merge the winner if it meets the minimum frequency.
Append the merge to the ordered table.
Stop when the budget is reached or no pair meets the minimum frequency.

variants.hint: The merge table is an ordered program.
variants.explanation: The ordered merge table is what encoding replays.

variants.title: Count the pairs
variants.context: pair_count(a, b) = sum over words of frequency × occurrences of the pair; weighted_tokens = sum of frequency × tokens in the current segmentation; compression = initial weighted tokens ÷ current weighted tokens.
variants.prompt: The corpus has “lower” with frequency 5 and “lowest” with frequency 3, both split into characters. What is the weighted count of the pair (l, o)?
variants.explanation: (l, o) appears once in each word: 5 × 1 + 3 × 1 = 8.

mistakes.feedback: Weight each occurrence by the word’s frequency.
That multiplies the two word frequencies. The pair occurs once in each word, so the weighted count is 5 + 3.

variants.title: Count the pairs
variants.context: pair_count(a, b) = sum over words of frequency × occurrences of the pair; weighted_tokens = sum of frequency × tokens in the current segmentation; compression = initial weighted tokens ÷ current weighted tokens.
variants.prompt: “low” (3 symbols) has frequency 10 and “lower” (5 symbols) has frequency 4. After merging (l, o) into one symbol, what is the weighted token count?
variants.hint: Recompute symbols per word after the merge, then weight.
variants.explanation: “low” becomes 2 symbols × 10 = 20; “lower” becomes 4 symbols × 4 = 16; total 36, down from 50.

mistakes.feedback: That is the count before the merge.
That adds the two frequencies and never multiplies each by the symbols the word has after the merge.

mistakes.feedback: The base alphabet is part of the vocabulary.

variants.title: Encode correctly
variants.context: Encoding replays the ranked merge program: same normalization, pre-tokenization, base symbols, merge ranks, special-token policy, and ID map. Do not tokenize greedily by longest match unless the specification says so.
variants.prompt: An implementation tokenizes by the longest vocabulary string that matches. Is that BPE?
options: Yes, if the vocabulary is sorted so the longest candidate is tried first.
Not standard BPE: segmentation replays merges in rank order, not by string length.
Yes; longest match is BPE, since both end at the same vocabulary entries.
optionFeedback: Sorting changes lookup order only. Merge rank decides segmentation, not candidate length.
Merge ranks decide, not string length.
Greedy longest match is a different algorithm. A longer item can lose to an earlier-ranked merge.
variants.explanation: Replay eligible merges in learned order until no ranked pair remains.

variants.title: Encode correctly
variants.context: Encoding replays the ranked merge program: same normalization, pre-tokenization, base symbols, merge ranks, special-token policy, and ID map. Do not tokenize greedily by longest match unless the specification says so.
variants.prompt: The same merges are applied in a different order. Does the model receive the same input?
options: Yes, because the same merge set produces the same final pieces either way.
Yes, as long as the vocabulary and ID map are unchanged between the two runs.
No. Merge order changes segmentation and therefore the IDs.
optionFeedback: Merges are not commutative. A later merge applied first consumes symbols an earlier one needed.
The same vocabulary can segment the same string differently once rank order is lost.
The ordered merge table is part of the contract.
variants.hint: Is the merge table a set or a program?
variants.explanation: The normalizer, boundary rules, ordered merge table, ID map, special tokens, and checkpoint form one contract.

variants.title: Encode correctly
variants.context: Encoding replays the ranked merge program: same normalization, pre-tokenization, base symbols, merge ranks, special-token policy, and ID map. Do not tokenize greedily by longest match unless the specification says so.
variants.prompt: A familiar piece such as “ing” is assigned a different ID in a rebuilt vocabulary. What happens at inference?
options: Nothing, since the surface spelling of the piece is unchanged in both vocabularies.
The model errors out, because the ID falls outside the embedding table it was trained on.
The model receives a different embedding for the same text and drifts silently.
optionFeedback: The model never sees spelling. It looks up a row by ID, and that row now holds a different vector.
The ID is still inside the table, so nothing raises. The lookup just returns the wrong embedding.
The model never sees the spelling, only the ID.
variants.explanation: Assigning a familiar piece a different ID changes what the model receives.

variants.title: Tell the families apart
variants.context: Word-level BPE starts from characters within pre-tokenized words with an end-of-word marker. Byte-level BPE maps bytes to a reversible alphabet and avoids a global unknown token. SentencePiece learns over raw text with whitespace markers.
variants.prompt: Arbitrary UTF-8 input must be representable with no global unknown token. Which family?
options: Byte-level BPE.
Word-level BPE with an unknown token.
Whole-word vocabulary.
optionFeedback: Bytes map to a reversible alphabet; rare scripts may expand into several pieces.
An unknown token is what byte fallback avoids.
Whole words cannot cover unseen text.
variants.explanation: Byte fallback covers rare input at the cost of longer sequences.

variants.title: Tell the families apart
variants.context: Word-level BPE starts from characters within pre-tokenized words with an end-of-word marker. Byte-level BPE maps bytes to a reversible alphabet and avoids a global unknown token. SentencePiece learns over raw text with whitespace markers.
variants.prompt: A tokenizer is trained on raw sentences with whitespace markers and no separate word tokenizer. Which family?
options: WordPiece.
SentencePiece BPE.
Word-level BPE.
optionFeedback: WordPiece uses its own continuation markers.
SentencePiece learns over a representation that includes whitespace markers.
Word-level BPE relies on a pre-tokenizer.
variants.hint: Does the tokenizer assume spaces separate words?
variants.explanation: Its normalization is still an explicit contract.

variants.title: Tell the families apart
variants.context: Word-level BPE starts from characters within pre-tokenized words with an end-of-word marker. Byte-level BPE maps bytes to a reversible alphabet and avoids a global unknown token. SentencePiece learns over raw text with whitespace markers.
variants.prompt: Two libraries print the same token strings. Are the token IDs and behavior identical?
options: Yes, since identical printed pieces mean identical vocabulary entries.
Yes, if both libraries describe their tokenizer as BPE with the same vocabulary size.
Not necessarily; normalization, unknown handling, and ID maps can differ.
optionFeedback: Two libraries can print the same piece and map it to different integers, which is what the model reads.
The name BPE plus a size is not a specification. Normalization and boundary rules still differ.
Similar-looking strings do not imply identical contracts.
variants.hint: What besides the string defines a token?
variants.explanation: Name the exact implementation and artifact versions.

variants.title: Weigh the budget
variants.context: A larger vocabulary lowers tokens per input for frequent slices but adds embedding rows and output-logit capacity, and rare tokens receive fewer training updates. BPE optimizes pair frequency, not morphology or downstream accuracy.
variants.prompt: Doubling the vocabulary shortens common English sequences. What does it cost?
options: More embedding rows and output logits, and rare tokens get fewer training updates.
Nothing, because the extra rows are only touched when those tokens actually appear.
Longer sequences, since more merges must be applied before encoding finishes.
optionFeedback: Every extra token costs model capacity and learns from fewer examples.
The output softmax spans every row on every step, so unused entries still cost capacity.
More merges make sequences shorter. The cost lands on model width, not sequence length.
variants.hint: What does each vocabulary entry consume?
variants.explanation: Compare candidate budgets with the target architecture and training-token budget.

variants.title: Weigh the budget
variants.context: A larger vocabulary lowers tokens per input for frequent slices but adds embedding rows and output-logit capacity, and rare tokens receive fewer training updates. BPE optimizes pair frequency, not morphology or downstream accuracy.
variants.prompt: A domain term became one token while a common word in another language is still five tokens. Why?
options: BPE optimizes pair frequency on its training corpus, not fairness across languages.
The algorithm recognizes domain terms and keeps them whole as meaningful units.
The other language is morphologically harder, so it cannot be compressed further.
optionFeedback: Vocabulary allocation follows training data.
BPE has no notion of meaning or morphology. It only counts adjacent pair frequency.
Morphology matters only through frequency. Raise that corpus share and the merges appear.
variants.explanation: Sample the corpus by language, script, and domain instead of one global average.

variants.prompt: Can the merge table be changed after the model is trained?
options: Yes, if the new table compresses the corpus into fewer tokens per document.
Not safely without retraining or compatibility evidence.
Yes, freely, because the merge table lives outside the model weights.
optionFeedback: Better compression can still hurt the model, because it moves boundaries the weights learned.
The merge table is part of the model’s contract.
It sits outside the weights but decides which rows they see, so it changes the input.
variants.hint: What does the model expect as input?
variants.explanation: Better corpus compression can hurt a model if boundaries or IDs change.
